checkpoints: Both Vite and Next.js build React applications, so this is not a "React vs Next.js" question — it's two different ways to build a React app.
Vite genuinely has a very fast dev server: HMR is near-instant because it serves source over native ES modules and pre-bundles with esbuild — that is developer speed.
"Fast to develop on" is not the same as "fast for the user to see content."

With a default Vite setup, the first HTTP response is almost empty (just a div#root plus a script tag); the UI only appears after the browser downloads and runs the JS bundle, and data is usually fetched afterward inside useEffect, adding another round trip.
An SEO crawler reading that empty HTML sees no product name, price, or description at all.

Next.js is the opposite: the server renders full HTML (SSR/SSG/RSC) before sending the response, so content is already in the first document, and the client only hydrates afterward to attach interactivity.

The root distinction is build tool vs framework: Vite is unopinionated — you assemble routing, data fetching, and rendering yourself — while Next.js ships file-based routing, server rendering, and build optimisation as ready-made conventions.

"Which one is faster" depends on which metric is measured: CSR has a fast TTFB but late FCP/LCP and empty HTML for crawlers, while server rendering trades a slightly higher TTFB for content already present at the very first paint.
In the App Router, every component is a Server Component by default — it runs exactly once on the server and has full backend access.

A Server Component can be an async function that awaits a database query or API call directly in its body, with no useEffect, no loading flag for the first render, and no client-to-server round trip after the page has painted.

What crosses the wire for a Server Component is not its code but a serialized description of its rendered output (the RSC payload) plus already-streamed HTML — zero client-side JavaScript for that part.
The cost is that a Server Component can never use useState, useEffect, event handlers, or any browser API, because it has no client lifecycle.

Writing 'use client' at the top of a file does not mark a single component in isolation — it marks the start of an entire client subtree: that file and everything it imports get compiled into a JS bundle, shipped to the browser, and hydrated.
In exchange for state and interactivity via 'use client', you pay in bundle weight and hydration cost.
Because the directive spreads through the whole import graph, placing it too high (a layout, a large wrapper) drags the entire subtree into client code and erases the zero-JS benefit.
The rule that follows: push 'use client' down as low as possible, right to the interactive leaf, so that read-only ancestor components stay on the server at zero cost.
Two things are wrong here and they are not the same severity — one is a genuine security hazard, the other is an architecture regression that merely "still works"; neither should merge as-is.

Because page.tsx now carries 'use client', everything it imports — including lib/db.ts, which has no server-only guard — is resolved into the client bundle, so nothing stops DATABASE_URL and the MOCK_PRODUCTS literal from shipping in a JS chunk to every visitor.

CI stays green because there is no build-time signal for this leak at all — it is a silent runtime leak, not a broken build — so the fix is adding import "server-only" to lib/db.ts to make the same mistake a loud compile-time failure next time.

'use client' marks an entry point for the whole subtree, not one component, so putting it at the page's top level pulls the read-only product name and price into the client bundle right alongside the button, erasing the zero-JS server render for the sake of one useState.

The previous inline await db.query() (which shipped ready HTML on first paint) was replaced by a useEffect fetch, so the page now renders an empty/loading shell first and fetches client-side, resurrecting the waterfall the Server Component model exists to remove.

Restructure to request: revert page.tsx to an async Server Component with no directive awaiting getProduct() inline, and carve AddToCartButton into the only 'use client' leaf, with only a serializable value (productId or resolved fields) crossing into it while the read-only description stays server-rendered.

Guardrail for next quarter: add import "server-only" to every module touching a secret or DB client so a client import fails the build, and treat a page- or layout-level 'use client' as needing explicit justification in review rather than a default choice.

Acceptance proof before re-approving: the build fails if any client file imports lib/db.ts, no downloaded client chunk contains DATABASE_URL or MOCK_PRODUCTS, view-source shows the product name/price as real server HTML again, and the Add-to-cart button still hydrates with its count incrementing on click.
A Suspense boundary resolves in an all-or-nothing way — it only stops showing its fallback once every suspended child inside it is ready.

This page has exactly one boundary wrapping all three widgets, so even though Quick finishes its data at 50ms, the user still stares at a spinner until Slow finishes at 1500ms — Quick's early completion is effectively wasted.
The fix is structural, not a data-layer change: give each independent data source its own Suspense boundary with its own fallback.

Splitting the boundary does not change the actual total wait (Slow still takes ~1500ms); it only changes how that wait is displayed, with Quick, Medium, and Slow each swapping in at their own time (~50ms/~500ms/~1500ms) independent of the others.

Layout stability matters: a small spinner swapping into full-height cards causes a large cumulative layout shift, so the fix is a per-widget skeleton sized to match the real card (same height, same content lines) so the swap doesn't push other elements.

Boundary granularity should be one per independent data source, not per tiny element — over-splitting produces a "popcorn effect" of scattered fragments plus overhead, while data meant to appear together should stay in one boundary.

Verification should rely on measurement, not feeling: throttled network shows chunks arriving in the correct order, data-testids confirm the widgets reveal at 50/500/1500ms, CLS measures near zero, and Slow still takes ~1500ms — proving the win is entirely in perceived speed with total latency unchanged.

Cost diagnosis: correctly names BOTH causes together — `force-dynamic` AND the in-body `cookies()` call — as what forces the entire route (not just the cart badge) to fully server-render before any byte is sent.
Structural fix — isolate: moves the `cookies()` read into its own async `CartCount` Server Component child, wrapped in `<Suspense fallback={<CartFallback />}>` with a skeleton fallback.
Structural fix — cleanup: explicitly deletes `export const dynamic = "force-dynamic"` as a required step (not merely implied by adding Suspense).
Names the global config switch: `experimental.ppr = "incremental"` set in `next.config`, and states it is off by default / opt-in at the app level.
Names the per-route config switch: `export const experimental_ppr = true`, and states it is a separate, explicit opt-in that the global flag alone does not provide.

Resulting behavior: states the build prerenders the shell (hero + fallback) as a static, CDN-servable page, AND that only the cart-count hole streams into its slot at request time over the same connection (no second round trip).

Guardrail: names at least one concrete silent-misconfiguration risk — e.g. another request-time read left outside a Suspense boundary re-flipping the whole route to dynamic, or a missing per-route `experimental_ppr` flag being a silent no-op under incremental mode.

Proof: names a concrete, checkable verification signal for the fix — e.g. the build output marking the route with the partial-prerender indicator, or TTFB/first-response-bytes showing the static shell serving identically while only the badge changes across two requests.

The concrete contract: `createComment(prev: CreateCommentState, formData: FormData): Promise<CreateCommentState>` with `CreateCommentState = { error: string | null }` — and every field in that state must be JSON-serializable, since it crosses the server/client action boundary on each round trip.

That signature isn't chosen freely — it's imposed by the action-state hook (`useFormState`/`useActionState`): the hook threads the previous run's returned state into the first parameter, and the framework hands the submitted form data into the second parameter as `FormData`.

Validation runs by parsing `formData` through a schema (Zod) RIGHT INSIDE the action, on the server, because a compiled action becomes a publicly callable RPC endpoint, so client-side validation is only UX, never the real trust boundary.

The return-vs-throw boundary: on a parse failure, RETURN `{ error: message }` so the hook re-renders the form with the error inline and per-field detail survives; throwing is reserved for unexpected failures, which is the error boundary's job, not form state's.

On success: persist the data, call `revalidatePath` on the route that renders the list (the action owns its own cache-invalidation consequence — the write alone invalidates nothing), then return `{ error: null }`.
Form-side guarantee A: bind the action to the `<form>`'s `action` attribute so a native POST still works before hydration or without JS, and every field carries a `name` matching a schema key.
Form-side guarantee B: inputs stay uncontrolled, and the submit button lives in a child component that reads the form's pending flag.
Defense against "just throw on bad input": a thrown validation error skips the form entirely, lands on an error page, and loses exactly the field-level context the user needs to fix their input.

Default rule: draw every region as a Server Component by default and only carve out a `'use client'` island where the page must react to `useState`/`onClick` right now — header/nav, product info, and reviews list stay Server Components that `await` data inline (no `useEffect`, no client fetch waterfall) and ship as HTML with zero JavaScript.

Only the add-to-cart + quantity picker earns a client island, because it's the only node that owns local interactive state — that single island is the entire JS-bundle line item for the route; every other node is free.

Only serializable data crosses into that island — e.g. `productId` as a `string`, a resolved `price` — never a closure or class instance, because props are encoded into the RSC payload and decoded in the browser and live code can't survive that trip.

The add-to-cart mutation itself doesn't need to become client logic just because the button is a client node — it can still cross as a server-function reference, so the actual write executes on the server.

The data-access module carries `import 'server-only'` as a compile-time wall, not just a comment, so any client-file import of it fails the build immediately, turning "did a secret leak?" into a guarantee instead of a hope.

The reviews list, being the slower region, gets its own Suspense boundary with a skeleton shaped like the loaded reviews, so a slow third-party service never gates the already-ready product info — the boundary map and the streaming map are the same drawing.

The theme provider must be `'use client'` to hold theme state yet sits at the very top wrapping everything; this is resolved via the `children`-slot pattern (the server root layout renders the rest of the tree and passes it into the client `ThemeProvider` as `children`) — which only works because composition is one-way: a Server Component may render a Client Component as a child, but never the reverse, since there is no server environment left once it runs in the browser.

On trade-off pressure (e.g. the quantity picker needing live stock), the senior move is to pass the resolved stock value down as data or re-check it inside the server-function mutation on submit, rather than promoting surrounding regions to client — the same bias applies to any later interactive need: prefer a second small leaf island over lifting the directive higher up the tree.

For the internal dashboard, pick a Vite SPA (CSR): it lives behind a login, no search engine will ever crawl it, and an empty-shell CSR app served from a static host covers the whole need — reaching for Next.js would only buy a server runtime and file-based routing conventions the app has no use for.
The cost accepted for the dashboard is that routing, data fetching, and state now have to be assembled by hand instead of coming built in.

For the public storefront, pick Next.js: a search-engine crawler reads whatever the server first returns, and a default Vite SPA returns an almost-empty `<div id="root">` with no product name/price yet, whereas Next.js's SSR/SSG renders that content into the HTML before it ever leaves the server.

For a catalog that changes only a few times a day, neither SSR nor plain SSG is the sweet spot: SSR would needlessly re-render on every single request despite barely-moving data, and pure SSG would go stale until the next full build.

ISR sits exactly between the two: the page is served as a static file, but Next.js rebuilds it in the background on a revalidate interval, so it stays close to fresh without paying a per-request render cost.
The hidden cost of Next.js's SSR/RSC path is that it needs a Node runtime somewhere — it's no longer a purely static deployment.

The decision axis throughout is the same: pick whichever tool's default already matches the primary need, not whichever sounds faster in the abstract, and remember the line isn't a hard wall since Vite can bolt on SSR and Next.js can still render individual routes on the client.

Root cause: `page.tsx` (or something above it) `await`s the slow data before emitting any JSX at all, so nothing can stream yet — traditional SSR is always all-or-nothing, and TTFB is gated by the slowest source.

The fix: since header/nav is static JSX, `page.tsx` renders synchronously with no `await`; each widget is split into its own async Server Component whose `await` lives INSIDE its own Suspense boundary, not inside `page.tsx`.

Streaming behavior: React suspends each boundary independently — chunk 1 is the shell plus three skeleton fallbacks sent almost immediately (0ms–~100ms shows the full layout with placeholders); out-of-order chunks then patch each skeleton as its data resolves (~50ms, ~500ms, ~1500ms) over one open HTTP response, with the three `await`s running concurrently so total wait is ~1500ms, not the sum of all three.

The navigation moment itself — from click until `/dashboard`'s server tree resolves — is covered by a route-level `loading.tsx`, which is convention sugar for a Suspense wrapping the whole page, distinct from the in-page boundaries that only cover their own widget; in practice both are needed.

Granularity rule: one boundary per INDEPENDENT data source — don't give every tiny stat its own boundary, because too many small boundaries cause a "popcorn" pop-in effect; group data that needs to appear together under one boundary instead.
Fallback skeletons must match the final layout's dimensions to avoid CLS on swap.
Caveat: streaming needs a streaming-capable runtime (Node/edge), not a plain static file host.
A route handler for an internal mutation forces you to hand-write three things the framework already provides: a POST handler, a client fetch layer, and a way to refresh the UI.

A Server Action folds all three into one: marking a function 'use server' makes Next.js create a hidden endpoint and inject only a REFERENCE into the client bundle (so the function body — and any DB/secret access inside it — never ships to the browser); calling the action then POSTs the serialized arguments to that hidden endpoint, the server runs the real function, and returns a serializable value back.
Binding an action directly to <form action={...}> gives progressive enhancement — the form submits even before JavaScript hydrates — which a fetch-based call can never do.

The choice between action and route handler is about WHO calls the mutation: internal-only calls (form submit, toggle, delete) use an action; a public HTTP contract for external clients (mobile, webhook, third-party) or fine-grained control over method/header/status/CORS still needs a real route handler, because an action is an internal RPC, not a public API.
The cost of using an action is the serialization constraint: every argument and return value must be serializable — no functions, class instances, or closures capturing non-serializable state.

After a write, the old UI stays in place because Next.js caches the route's rendered result, so you must explicitly tell the framework what's stale rather than expecting the write itself to refresh the UI.

revalidatePath marks the route stale without re-fetching inside the action itself — it's the next render that recomputes the stale part, so the Server Component reruns, reads the updated store, and ships fresh HTML.

revalidatePath invalidates the whole route (simple but coarse), while revalidateTag invalidates only the tagged data — choose a tag when only specific data changed, and a path when the whole route depends on that change.
